6.14

C. Modal verbs: dürfen | sollen

These two modal verbs function structurally just like können, müssen and wollen, but require special attention to their meanings.


C.1

Dürfen


dürfen to be allowed to; may (permission)

singular

plural

first-person

ich darf

wir dürfen

second-person

du darfst [familiar]

Sie dürfen [formal]

ihr dürft [familiar]

Sie dürfen [formal]

third-person

er/sein Bruder darf

sie/seine Schwester darf

es/das Kind darf

sie/die Leute dürfen

Notice that this verb means to be allowed, rather than to allow – i.e., it denotes permission granted to the sentence subject, rather than the subject’s granting of permission. (To express I allow you to do that, German uses the verb lassen, which will be introduced later.)

Some examples:

Seniors dürfen drei Kurse im letzten Semester machen.

Seniors are allowed to take three courses in the last semester.

Darf ich fragen, was eine »P-rade« ist?

May I ask what a “P-rade” is?

Du darfst keine Kerzen° in deinem Zimmer haben!

You’re not allowed to have any candles in your room!

Darf man auf Cannon Green Croquet spielen?

Are you allowed to play croquet on Cannon Green?

content:
C.2

Sollen


sollen to be supposed to, to be expected to; should

singular

plural

first-person

ich soll

wir sollen

second-person

du sollst [familiar]

Sie sollen [formal]

ihr sollt [familiar]

Sie sollen [formal]

third-person

er /der Student soll

sie/die Uni soll

es/das Problem soll

sie/die Professoren sollen

Where dürfen clarifies a potential ambiguity in English, sollen introduces one. Consider the difference in English between should and to be supposed to:

I should do that.

I’m supposed to/expected to do that.

Not quite the same, are they? But sollen is used in colloquial German to express both of them: Ich soll das machen is an acceptable translation of both sentences above.

To make the distinction between I’m expected to and I think I should, German speakers frequently make use of a subjunctive form of sollen (which will be discussed in detail later) to convey a personal sense of responsibility on the speaker’s part, as opposed to external pressure:

Ich sollte das machen.

Here’s a rule of thumb: If your intention is to express the idea that someone said I’m supposed to do this, then use soll. If the meaning is simply I think this is what I should do, you can use either soll or sollte. The forms for sollte are similar to soll: first- and third-person singular are sollte, and the rest take the expected endings: solltest / sollten / solltet.

D.1

Mögen


You already know that mögen means to like, as in Ich mag diese Musik. Now that you’ve encountered other modal verbs, you can see that the vowel change from mögen to mag as well as the lack of a verb ending for ich mag / er mag / sie mag are typical for modal verbs:


mögen to like

singular

plural

first-person

ich mag

wir mögen

second-person

du magst [familiar]

Sie mögen [formal]

ihr mögt [familiar]

Sie mögen [formal]

third-person

er /der Junge mag

sie/die Frau mag

es/das Kind mag

sie/die Eltern mögen
D.1
label: D.1

content:
D.2

Möchte


When you want to say I like [X], you can use mögen (to like) or its subjunctive form möchte (would like) by itself, with a direct object. Möchte is also used frequently in V1-V2 structures to express the meaning would like to, with an infinitive at the end of the clause.

Even though the subjunctive mood hasn't been introduced yet, möchte is used so frequently that you should learn its forms now:


möcht- would like (to)

singular

plural

first-person

ich möchte

wir möchten

second-person

du möchtest [familiar]

Sie möchten [formal]

ihr möchtet [familiar]

Sie möchten [formal]

third-person

er /der Junge möchte

sie /die Frau möchte

es /das Kind möchte

sie/die Eltern möchten

A few examples:

Ich möchte eine Katze.

Was möchtest du heute machen?

Möchten Sie eine Tasse Kaffee?

Er möchte wohl etwas länger schlafen.

I would like a cat.

What would you like to do today?

Would you like a cup of coffee?

He probably would like to sleep a little longer.

content:
D.3

A bit of etiquette concerning mögen / möchte / wollen:

All three of these modals can stand alone with a direct object:

Ich mag diese Pizza.

Ich möchte ein Stück Pizza.

Ich will ein Stück Pizza.

I like this pizza.

I’d like a piece of pizza.

I want a piece of pizza.

While all of these are grammatically correct, the last one (Ich will …) can come across as quite blunt in situations involving requests — a bit like someone who insists I want that!

When requesting something (say, in a restaurant), use möchte or (as you learned in chapter 4) hätte gern:

Ich möchte noch eine Tasse Kaffee, bitte!

Ich hätte gern ein Stück Apfeltorte.

Wollen is perfectly acceptable, however, when it’s used in conjunction with another verb to express what you want to do, as is möchten, if you’d prefer to say what you’d like to do.
